nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to C$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes $L$ through a subset $A \subseteq C$. If $\varphi = f \circ \psi$ for monoid morphisms $\psi : \Sigma^* \to T$ and $f : T \to C$, then $\psi$ recognizes $L$ through the preimage $f^{-1}(A)$.
nodes.title: Recognition pulls back along a factorization

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A_1 \subseteq M$. If $A_2 \subseteq M$ satisfies $\varphi(x) \in A_1 \iff \varphi(x) \in A_2$ for every word $x$, then $\varphi$ also recognizes $L$ through $A_2$.
nodes.title: Changing the accepting set off the image of a recognizer

nodes.summary: If the syntactic monoid of a language $L$ is finite, then the syntactic DFA of $L$ has finitely many states and accepts exactly $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA of a language with finite syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Every language accepted by a DFA with finitely many states has a finite syntactic monoid.
nodes.title: Languages of finite automata have finite syntactic monoids

nodes.summary: If a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to a finite monoid $M$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through some subset of $M$, then the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.
nodes.title: Finite recognizers give finite syntactic monoids

nodes.summary: Every language whose syntactic monoid is finite is regular.
nodes.title: Finite syntactic monoid implies regularity

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, $x \in L$ if and only if the image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$ lies in the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$, the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes the language

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language. For all words $x$ and $y$, if the syntactic morphism of $L$ sends $x$ and $y$ to the same element of the syntactic monoid of $L$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same Nerode class with respect to $L$.
nodes.title: Equal syntactic classes give equal Nerode classes

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A \subseteq M$. Then the canonical monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$, is surjective.
nodes.title: The image of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A \subseteq M$. This is the monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$ for every word $x$. It is well defined because words with the same image under $\varphi$ are syntactically…
nodes.title: Map from a recognizer's image to the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its codomain, then the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$: any words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Recognizer kernels refine the syntactic congruence

nodes.summary: If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its codomain, then the canonical monoid morphism from the quotient of $\Sigma^*$ by the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends the class of a word $x$ to its syntactic class, is surjective.
nodes.title: The kernel quotient of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$ be such that $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$. Since the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ (words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$) is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$, there is a monoid morphism from the quotient of…
nodes.title: Canonical map from a recognizer's kernel quotient to the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ if and only if the set of words of $\Sigma^*$ that belong to $L$ equals $\varphi^{-1}(A)$.
nodes.title: Recognition as an inverse image

nodes.summary: For every language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, recognizes $L$ through the accepting subset of the syntactic monoid, namely the set of syntactic classes of words in $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes its language

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ with state set $Q$, start state $q_0$ and set of accepting states $F$. The transition morphism of $M$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the monoid of state transformations of $Q$, recognizes the language accepted by $M$ through the set of transformations $f$ with $f(q_0) \in F$.
nodes.title: The transition morphism of a DFA recognizes its language

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ when, for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$, $w \in L$ if and only if $\varphi(w) \in A$.
nodes.title: Recognition of a language by a monoid morphism

nodes.summary: For a type $Q$ of states, the bijection from the state transformations of $Q$ to the functions $Q \to Q$ that sends each transformation to its underlying function; it forgets the multiplication of state transformations.
nodes.title: State transformations as functions

nodes.summary: For a type $Q$ of states, the state transformation monoid of $Q$ consists of all functions $Q \to Q$, multiplied by composition in the opposite order: the product $fg$ first applies $f$ and then $g$, so $(fg)(q) = g(f(q))$, and the unit is the identity function.
nodes.title: State transformation monoid

nodes.summary: For a language $L$, the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$ is the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$: a class belongs to it when its representatives lie in $L$, which does not depend on the representative chosen.
nodes.title: Accepting set of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The image of the action of the syntactic monoid of $L$ on the states of $M$, the monoid homomorphism sending the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the state transformation induced by reading $x$, is exactly the transition monoid of $M$.
nodes.title: Image of the syntactic action

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA with state type $Q$, and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. This is the monoid homomorphism from the syntactic monoid of $L$ to the state transformation monoid of $Q$ that sends the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the map taking each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ by reading $x$. It is well defined because syntactically equivalent words act…
nodes.title: Action of the syntactic monoid on states

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The syntactic congruence of $L$ equals the kernel of the transition morphism of $M$: two words are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they induce the same transformation of the states of $M$.
nodes.title: Syntactic congruence as a kernel

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic congruence of $L$ is the monoid congruence on the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that relates words $x$ and $y$ when, for all words $u$ and $v$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic congruence

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, the syntactic DFA of $L$ accepts exactly $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA accepts its language

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, every state of the syntactic DFA of $L$ is reachable: some word leads to it from the start state.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA is accessible

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every state $q$ of the syntactic DFA of $L$ (an element of the syntactic monoid of $L$) and every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, the state reached from $q$ by reading $x$ is $q \cdot [x]$, where $[x]$ is the image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$.
nodes.title: Runs of the syntactic DFA

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The syntactic DFA of $L$ has the syntactic monoid of $L$ as its set of states, the identity $1$ as start state, and the syntactic classes of the words of $L$ as accepting states; from a state $q$, reading a letter $a \in \Sigma$ leads to $q \cdot [a]$, where $[a]$ is the syntactic class of the one-letter word $a$.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic monoid of $L$ is the quotient of the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words by the syntactic congruence of $L$, which relates words $x$ and $y$ when $uxv \in L \iff uyv \in L$ for all words $u$ and $v$.
nodes.title: Syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$ is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends each word to its class under the syntactic congruence of $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic morphism

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $w, x, y, z \in \Sigma^*$ be words. If $w$ and $x$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, and $y$ and $z$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $wy$ and $xz$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence is compatible with concatenation

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ that is accessible (every state is reached from the start state by some word) and state-separated (distinct states have distinct continuation languages), and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. Then two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, running $M$ from $q$ on…
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence via transition actions

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.
nodes.title: Syntactically equivalent words agree on membership

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then they are Nerode equivalent for $L$: the sets $\{z : xz \in L\}$ and $\{z : yz \in L\}$ are equal.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence refines Nerode equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a set $A \subseteq M$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$: for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.
nodes.title: Words with equal recognizer images are syntactically equivalent

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ have the same transition action on $M$, that is, for every state $q$, running $M$ from $q$ on $x$ ends in the same state as running $M$ from $q$ on $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Words with the same transition action are syntactically equivalent

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $wx$ and $wy$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence is stable under left multiplication

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xw$ and $yw$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence is stable under right multiplication

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ when, for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Each word $x \in \Sigma^*$ determines the element of the transition monoid of $M$ given by the state transformation that sends each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ after reading $x$.
nodes.title: Transition monoid element of a word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that is accessible (every state is reachable from the start state) and state-separated (two states with the same continuation language are equal). If two words $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for the language accepted by $M$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, reading $x$ from $q$ and reading $y$ from $q$ lead to the same state.
nodes.title: Syntactically equivalent words act identically

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition action of $x$ is the map sending each state $q$ of $M$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ starting from $q$.
nodes.title: Transition action of a word

nodes.summary: The transition monoid of a DFA $M$ is the image of the transition morphism of $M$: the submonoid of state transformations of $M$ consisting of the transition actions of all words, where a word $x$ acts by sending each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$.
nodes.title: Transition monoid of a DFA

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$, the transition morphism is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid of words to the state transformations of $M$ that sends each word $x$ to its transition action, the map taking each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$; with this order, the word $xy$ is sent to…
nodes.title: Transition morphism of a DFA

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition transformation of $x$ is the transition action of $x$, the map sending each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$, regarded as an element of the monoid of state transformations of $M$ (multiplied in reading order: $fg$ applies $f$ first, then $g$).
nodes.title: Transition transformation of a word
Theory of Computation

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
